strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: universal multimodal embeddings for digital pathology, moving beyond task-specific models and labor-intensive annotations.
Introduces PMEB, a multi-task benchmark covering retrieval, composed retrieval, and classification, which can support standardized evaluation of pathology multimodal embeddings.
Proposes MLLM4PUE, a framework that uses an MLLM with summarization prompts and LoRA-based contrastive fine-tuning to generate unified pathology image-text embeddings.

Provides extensive experiments across many datasets, comparing against CLIP-based and MLLM baselines, and shows consistent improvements on many retrieval, composed retrieval, and classification tasks.
Includes useful ablations on sample size (1k vs. full datasets) and embedding fusion methods, supporting efficiency and the benefit of prompt-based fusion.
Modality gap analysis via t-SNE provides additional evidence that the proposed embeddings align image and text modalities better than a CLIP-based baseline.
The paper is generally well-written and the figures/tables are informative.
weaknesses: Benchmark statistics are inconsistent: the abstract claims 16 tasks from 15 datasets, Table 1 caption says 15 tasks from 14 datasets, but the table itself lists 19 task rows and 15 datasets. There are also citation/reference errors (e.g., Databiox cited as [19], which is the CRC-100k reference). For a benchmark contribution, this undermines credibility.

Potential data leakage/overlap: MLLM4PUE-Q is trained on Quilt1M and evaluated on Quilt-VQA and Quilt-VQA-RED, which are derived from the Quilt source. No overlap analysis is provided, so the large gains on these datasets may be inflated by having seen related images or captions during training.

Comparison fairness is unclear: MLLM4PUE uses an 8B LLaVA-NeXT model, while the main baselines (PLIP, PathCLIP, QuiltNet) are much smaller CLIP-based models. The observed gains may partly come from model scale and general vision-language pretraining rather than the proposed framework. E5-V is not fine-tuned on pathology data, making it a weak MLLM baseline for the proposed fine-tuning strategy.

Limited technical novelty: the method largely adapts existing ideas (MLLM embedding extraction via summarization prompts, contrastive learning, LoRA fine-tuning) to the pathology domain. The main new element is the benchmark aggregation, which itself is composed of existing datasets rather than new annotations or a fundamentally new evaluation protocol.

Insufficient ablations: no control for backbone size, prompt design, loss function, or LoRA vs. full fine-tuning; no analysis of what the MLLM actually generates or whether the extracted last-token embedding is semantically meaningful.
No limitations or societal-impact discussion is included, and no statistical significance tests or error bars are reported for the main results.

Some claims are overstated, such as 'first time to explore re-purposing MLLM for extracting embeddings in pathology area' and 'comprehensive benchmark,' given prior work like E5-V and the benchmark's aggregated nature.

strengths: Targets a timely and important problem: moving digital pathology from task-specific models toward task-agnostic, universal multimodal embeddings, which is a well-motivated direction.

The evaluation spans a relatively broad set of downstream tasks (15 tasks over 14 datasets) grouped into retrieval, composed retrieval, and classification, and includes both image-to-text and text-to-image directions.

For the matched-training-data comparisons (MLLM4PUE-O vs PLIP on OpenPath, MLLM4PUE-P vs PathCLIP on PathCap, MLLM4PUE-Q vs QuiltNet on Quilt1M), the proposed model does improve over the corresponding CLIP baselines on most reported metrics (e.g., Table 2 i2t Arch-PubMed Recall@5: 0.105 vs 0.037; Table 3 Bach wF1: 0.561 vs 0.124).

Includes some useful supporting analyses: an ablation on the number of benchmark samples (Fig. 5) and a fusion-method ablation (Table 5) showing that jointly encoding image+question helps more than question-only or simple embedding addition.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty. The framework is essentially E5-V [18] adapted to pathology: an MLLM (LLaVA-NeXT-8B) is prompted to 'summarize in one word' and fine-tuned with a standard InfoNCE contrastive loss using LoRA. There is no new architecture, loss, or conceptual insight; the claimed difference from E5-V (LoRA fine-tuning on existing pathology image-text pairs instead of a domain-specific instruction-tuned LLM) is an incremental engineering delta.

The benchmark contribution (PMEB) is largely a repackaging of existing public datasets, reformulated as embedding-style tasks; classification is just standard zero-shot CLIP-style evaluation with class-name templates. The 'comprehensive benchmark' claim is overstated, and subsampling large datasets to 1,000 samples further reduces rigor.

Confounded/unfair comparisons. MLLM4PUE is trained on ~594K pairs (union of OpenPath, PathCap, Quilt1M), while each CLIP baseline is trained on a single one of these datasets. Headline claims that the model 'consistently surpasses baseline methods' conflate increased training data/capacity with the method itself, and no CLIP-style or LLM baseline of comparable data/capacity is provided.

The E5-V baseline is knowingly run in a weak regime: the paper itself states E5-V requires a domain-specific pathology LLM, yet it is evaluated without pathology adaptation, so its poor scores inflate the apparent gains. Similarly, no MLLM baseline without contrastive fine-tuning is included to isolate the contribution of the training recipe.

Serious train/test contamination risk that is not properly handled. Quilt-VQA / Quilt-VQA-RED are derived from Quilt-1M/Quilt-LLaVA, which is part of the training data (Quilt1M), and the paper only acknowledges an 'overlap' and uses ChatGPT for ad-hoc cleaning rather than principled decontamination. The large margins on Quilt-VQA (e.g., 0.475 vs 0.180) are therefore not trustworthy.

No discussion of practical cost. Extracting 'universal embeddings' from an 8B MLLM is far more expensive at inference than a CLIP-style dual encoder; this is a critical trade-off for the claimed universality and is not addressed.

The modality-gap argument (Fig. 4) is weakly motivated: it is not established that reducing the image-text gap improves downstream performance, and the reported gap values appear inconsistent with the visibly separated clusters shown in the t-SNE plots.

Missing important comparisons and statistical rigor: strong pathology vision-language foundation models (e.g., CONCH is only partially used, UNI/Virchow absent) are not compared on embedding tasks, and there are no error bars or significance tests despite many small-margin differences.

Presentation and correctness issues suggest insufficient care: citation errors (Table 5 labels Quilt-VQA as [12] instead of [35]), incorrect in-text table references (composed-retrieval results are in Table 4 but the text points to Table 3), typos ('conservative learning' in Sec. 3.3), and the absence of any limitations/failure-mode discussion.

strengths: Timely and novel direction: the paper is among the first to explore re-purposing a generative Multimodal LLM (LLaVA-NeXT-8B) to produce *unified* pathology image-text embeddings, rather than relying on separately encoded CLIP/CoCa-style modalities. This directly targets a real limitation of current pathology vision-language models (independent encoders, 74-token text limit).

A genuinely useful benchmark contribution: PMEB aggregates 15 original tasks from 14 datasets into three coherent meta-task categories (retrieval, composed retrieval, classification) and reformulates each task specifically for embedding evaluation (instructional prompt + query -> target selection). Standardized sampling (1,000 samples with preserved class distribution) and reproducibility details make it practically valuable.

Broad and consistent empirical evidence: MLLM4PUE outperforms PLIP, PathCLIP, QuiltNet and E5-V across most retrieval, classification and composed-retrieval tasks (Tables 2-4), and notably achieves these gains with fewer training samples than CONCH (0.2M vs 1.16M).

Well-designed ablations that support the claims: sample-size robustness (1k vs 3k/5k/full, Fig. 5), embedding-fusion study contrasting 'only question'/'add embedding'/'prompt' (Table 5), and a quantitative + qualitative modality-gap analysis via t-SNE and the ||Δ||_gap metric (Fig. 4). These go beyond simple leaderboard reporting.

Clear writing, good organization, and sufficiently detailed implementation notes (QLoRA, DeepSpeed ZeRO-2, temperature 0.02, 6×H100, batch 144, lr 4e-4) that support reproducibility and appropriate attribution of datasets.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core mechanism (a summarization prompt that distills the input into a single token and using the last-token embedding) closely follows E5-V [18]; the pathology adaptation is essentially LoRA fine-tuning with an InfoNCE loss. The specific 'in one word' prompt design and last-token pooling are asserted rather than ablated against alternatives (e.g., multi-token/mean pooling, longer summaries), and the single-token compression is intuitively lossy for gigapixel-scale pathology content.

Potential data contamination in the composed-retrieval evaluation: MLLM4PUE-Q is trained on Quilt1M [16], while the composed-retrieval benchmarks Quilt-VQA / Quilt-VQA-RED [35] originate from the same Quilt source. The unusually large gains of MLLM4PUE-Q on these tasks may partly reflect overlap rather than genuine cross-modal generalization, and this risk is not discussed or controlled for.

Questionable fairness of the E5-V baseline: reported numbers are implausibly low (e.g., Recall@5 = 0.006 on Arch-PubMed, ~0.067 on Arch-book), which the authors attribute to missing pathology fine-tuning. Given how much of the reported 'superiority' rests on this baseline, the discrepancy warrants verification (prompt/embedding-extraction mismatch is a plausible confound).

Incomplete comparison set: CONCH is compared only on classification, not on retrieval or composed retrieval, despite being a strong pathology vision-language model; vision-only pathology foundation models (e.g., UNI, Virchow, GigaPath) and their linear-probe performance are not considered. No efficiency/cost analysis is given for using an 8B MLLM versus CLIP-scale baselines, which matters for the 'sustainability' motivation in the abstract.

Overstated framing: the claim that MLLM4PUE 'consistently surpasses' baselines is not fully supported, since CONCH wins on some datasets (SkinCancer, Wsss4luad) and gains vary considerably across tasks. There is little error analysis or discussion of limitations/failure modes, and the 'benchmark' is largely an aggregation/reformulation of existing datasets rather than newly collected data.

strengths: The paper defines a clinically well-motivated task, Pathology Composed Retrieval (PCR), and argues convincingly that retrieval-as-'computational consult' is a more interpretable and trust-preserving alternative to black-box diagnostic prediction; the task definition (composed queries of interleaved images, text, and video against a large candidate pool) is natural for pathology practice.

A new benchmark is introduced spanning four composed-retrieval sub-tasks (multi-image→text, image+text→image, image+text→text, video→text) plus simple retrieval and zero-shot tile classification, with a clear statistics table (Table 1) covering many public pathology sources; this fills a genuine evaluation gap, since existing pathology datasets cannot measure compositional retrieval.

Empirical results are strong and consistent: HOMIE beats all pathology CLIP-based and general MLLM baselines on every composed-retrieval sub-task (e.g., 78.5 vs 43.0 R@1 for Multi-Image→Text on Bookset), while remaining competitive on simple retrieval and achieving best or near-best zero-shot tile classification on 8/9 datasets.

The two-stage framework cleanly separates two distinct problems (task mismatch: generative vs. metric learning; domain mismatch: natural vs. pathology images), and the pathology-specific ingredients (stain normalization/augmentation, native-resolution ViT with 2D-RoPE, progressive morphology→diagnosis curriculum, bootstrapped data filtering) are sensible and individually ablated.

Supporting analyses beyond leaderboard numbers are provided: an ablation of the prompt-guided fusion vs. naive embedding addition, a quantitative modality-gap metric with UMAP visualizations showing HOMIE's image/text embeddings are better aligned than PathGen-CLIP, MUSK, and CONCH, and a qualitative retrieval comparison.

The manuscript is clearly written and well organized, and the related-work section adequately positions the work relative to pathology CLIP models (CONCH, MUSK, PLIP, PathGen-CLIP) and MLLM-based embedding models (E5-V, VLM2Vec, GME, LamRA).
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is modest and somewhat over-claimed. The core recipe—using an EOL/summarization prompt to extract an embedding from an MLLM and adapting it for retrieval with text-only LoRA pre-training plus contrastive InfoNCE—closely follows E5-V [18], which the paper itself acknowledges. The contribution is largely domain-specific engineering on top of an existing adaptation scheme, and the paper would benefit from an explicit statement of what is new versus adopted.

The comparison against CLIP-based baselines may be unfair for the paper's central architectural claim. Baselines are restricted to 'parameter-free operations' (naive embedding addition) on the grounds that no compositional training data exists, yet HOMIE itself demonstrates composed generalization from purely bi-modal/single-modal training data. A dual-encoder baseline augmented with a trainable fusion module (MLP/cross-attention) trained on the same curated pairs is therefore feasible and would be the informative control; without it, the claim of an 'architectural deadlock' for CLIP-like models is overstated.

Video-to-text retrieval is effectively unevaluated against comparable methods: all pathology CLIP entries in Table 2 are '—' for the VideoPath task, so the claim of outperforming baselines there rests on very weak general-MLLM numbers (1.6–10.8 R@1). In addition, the architecture section does not explain how spatio-temporal video tokens are formed or fused by the native-resolution ViT, despite the task description emphasizing 'fusion of spatio-temporal features'.

Potential training/test data overlap is not audited. HOMIE is trained on PathGen-1.6M, PathCap, and 500K filtered Quilt-1M pairs, while the composed-retrieval test sets include Quilt-VQA / Quilt-VQA-RED (derived from the same Quilt video/instruction source) and PubMed-derived corpora (Pubmedset, MMUpubmed, Educontent) that resemble the training sources. The paper criticizes CONCH for benefiting from PubMed overlap on Pubmedset but does not examine whether its own gains on Quilt-VQA or PubMed-derived sets are partly attributable to the same effect.

Benchmark construction is under-specified in the main text. The candidate/negative pool sizes and how distractors are sampled for each retrieval task are not stated, nor is the sampling procedure behind the 'Selected samples' column. Using a single ground-truth positive per query with R@k is fragile in a clinical retrieval setting where many candidates may be equally relevant; some form of multi-positive or expert-judged relevance would substantially strengthen the evaluation. Details are deferred to the supplementary material, and public release/licensing of the benchmark is not stated, which limits reproducibility.

The related work omits the substantial literature on composed image retrieval in the general domain (e.g., Vo et al. CVPR 2019, Pic2Word, SEARLE, MagicLens, CompoDiff). Given that the paper's headline claim is to 'formally define' composed retrieval for pathology, the absence of this line of work weakens the framing and leaves unclear how the proposed task relates to prior compositional-retrieval formulations.

Ablation evidence is thinner than the text suggests. Differences such as 53.2 vs. 50.1 average R@1 and 72.5 vs. 71.6 tile accuracy are described as 'significant,' but no seeds, variance, or significance tests are reported, and the tile-classification gap in particular could easily be within run-to-run noise. The same applies to the fusion ablation, where a 'simple add' variant with a different prompt is not obviously a matched control.

There is no limitations or societal-impact discussion, which is conspicuous for a medical decision-support system. Issues such as dataset and stain bias across institutions, retrieval of clinically outdated or non-representative evidence, failure modes of embedding-based retrieval, and the risk of clinician over-reliance on retrieved cases are not addressed.

Some claims outrun the evidence: 'the first to generate a single, unified omni-modal embedding for pathology' is a strong priority claim supported mainly by the authors' own comparison set, and several 'general MLLM' baselines share the same Qwen2.5-VL-7B backbone as HOMIE, making the separation between 'backbone capability' and 'framework contribution' somewhat blurred.

strengths: The paper defines a novel and practically motivated task—Pathology Composed Retrieval (PCR)—that reflects real clinical workflows where pathologists query databases with interleaved multi-modal inputs (text, multiple images, video). This is a genuine gap in the literature, as existing pathology retrieval models (MUSK, CONCH, PathGen-CLIP, etc.) are constrained to dual-encoder image-text architectures and cannot handle compositional queries.

The proposed HOMIE framework is technically sound and well-motivated. The two-stage design directly targets the identified 'task mismatch' (via language-only retrieval adaptation) and 'domain mismatch' (via pathology-specific tuning with stain augmentation, native resolution processing, and a progressive knowledge curriculum). The curriculum from morphology (PathGen-1.6M) to diagnostic knowledge (PathCap, Quilt-1M) is a sensible and empirically validated choice.

The empirical evidence is strong and comprehensive. HOMIE substantially outperforms all baselines on the new PCR benchmark (e.g., 78.5% vs 43.8% R@1 on Multi-Image-to-Text) while matching or exceeding SOTA on traditional simple retrieval and zero-shot tile classification tasks. The results are consistently reported across multiple datasets (Bookset, Pubmedset, Educontent, MMUpubmed, Quilt-VQA, VideoPath) and multiple metrics (R@1/5/10, weighted accuracy).

The ablation studies (Tables 5 and 6) are informative and well-designed, isolating the contributions of data filtering, progressive curriculum, stain normalization, native resolution, and prompt-guided fusion. The prompt-guide vs. simple-add comparison convincingly demonstrates that the compositional fusion capability is an emergent property of the adapted MLLM rather than simple vector arithmetic.

The qualitative results (Figure 3) and UMAP modality-gap visualization (Figure 4) provide complementary, intuitive evidence for the central claim that HOMIE produces a more unified omni-modal embedding space. The quantitative modality-gap metric (0.325 vs. 0.393/0.571/0.874) supports the visual finding.

The paper is clearly written and well-organized. The problem framing (Section 1) and related work (Section 2) effectively motivate the contributions, and the methods are described with sufficient implementation detail (hyperparameters, LoRA configuration, batch sizes, learning rates) to support reproducibility. Training on public data only is a notable strength that strengthens the reproducibility and attribution case.
weaknesses: While the benchmark is a valuable contribution, several design choices could be better justified. Using GPT-5 to rephrase answers to prevent lexical-overlap 'cheating' is a reasonable heuristic, but the paper does not report validation that the rephrased queries are semantically equivalent or that this procedure does not introduce distributional artifacts. The data-filtering threshold λ used to bootstrap Quilt-1M is described qualitatively but the sensitivity to this hyperparameter is not analyzed.

The 'prompt guide' fusion mechanism is central to the paper's claims, yet its precise mechanics are somewhat underspecified. The paper states that the LLM produces a unified embedding via an EOL prompt, but does not fully characterize how interleaved multi-modal tokens are ordered, how the model behaves with varying numbers of images, or whether performance degrades gracefully with very long composed queries.

The clinical relevance claim ('computational consult', expert-guided decision support) is compelling in motivation but is not empirically validated with pathologist-in-the-loop evaluation or downstream diagnostic outcomes. This is a limitation of the current study rather than a flaw, but the paper could be clearer about the gap between retrieval quality and clinical utility.

Some evaluation splits are relatively small (e.g., VideoPath 244 samples, Quilt-VQA 252 samples), which limits statistical confidence in those particular results. Additionally, the baseline comparison for compositional tasks relies on parameter-free embedding addition for CLIP-based models; while the authors justify this by the lack of compositional training data, a stronger fusion baseline (e.g., learned MLP with synthetic pairs) would make the comparison more convincing.

The paper does not discuss potential negative societal impacts or deployment risks (e.g., over-reliance on retrieval results, privacy of patient data in databases, bias across demographic groups), which would be appropriate given the clinical framing. Limitations and failure modes are only briefly touched upon in the conclusion.

strengths: Addresses an important and under-explored problem: retrieval-based clinical decision support in pathology, with a clear motivation for transparency over black-box diagnosis.

Defines the Pathology Composed Retrieval (PCR) task and introduces a benchmark covering multi-image, image-text, and video-text retrieval, plus simple retrieval and tile classification, which could facilitate future work if properly validated.

The HOMIE framework is reasonably engineered, combining an MLLM backbone with native-resolution vision encoding, stain augmentation/normalization, progressive curriculum, and prompt-guided embedding extraction.

Experiments include many baselines from pathology CLIP-based models and general MLLM retrieval models, with zero-shot composed retrieval, simple retrieval, tile classification, ablations, and qualitative/UMAP analyses.
The paper is generally well organized and the figures/tables communicate the main claims clearly, though several claims need qualification.
weaknesses: The benchmark is not rigorously validated: queries and answers are generated/rephrased using GPT-5 without pathologist verification, tasks such as Image-Text-to-Text are repurposed from VQA with potentially ambiguous ground truth, and the composed retrieval test sets are very small (e.g., 244-724 samples), making metrics unstable.

Potential train/test data leakage is not addressed. HOMIE is trained on Quilt-1M, PathCap, and PathGen-1.6M, while evaluation uses Quilt-VQA, Quilt-VQA-RED, and Bookset; Quilt-VQA is likely derived from Quilt-1M, and no disjointness check or split protocol is reported.

The 'zero-shot' characterization is misleading. HOMIE is fine-tuned on large pathology text and image-text corpora, while the compared general MLLMs are not adapted on the same data, and CLIP-based baselines are artificially restricted to parameter-free embedding addition, making the comparisons unfair.

The claim that HOMIE 'matches SOTA' on traditional retrieval is not consistently supported: on Pubmedset and EduContent R@1, it trails CONCH and other baselines; the paper explains only CONCH's advantage on Pubmedset and does not fully account for other gaps.

The two-stage design is not adequately ablated. There is no ablation for stage-one language-only training, the choice of the last hidden state before <emb>, the LoRA configuration, or the MLLM backbone, so the central 'dual mismatch' solution is not convincingly isolated.

Ablation results are weak or inconsistent with the claims. Stain normalization/augmentation changes composed retrieval by only 0.1 and tile classification by 0.6, yet is described as crucial; no error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple seeds are provided for any result.

Important implementation details are missing, including data-filtering threshold lambda, GPT-5 prompts, LoRA rank/alpha/dropout, optimizer/scheduler details, exact training data splits, and the zero-shot tile-classification protocol (e.g., whether a classifier is trained or text prompts are used).

The technical novelty is incremental: the core method adapts existing MLLM-based embedding/retrieval approaches (e.g., E5-V, VLM2Vec, GME) to pathology via domain-specific tuning; the main novel component is the benchmark, which has validity concerns.

The paper lacks comparison to composed image retrieval methods from the broader vision community, despite defining a composed retrieval task; this weakens the claim that the architecture is necessary for composition.

The clinical relevance is asserted but not demonstrated: there is no pathologist user study, no evaluation of diagnostic utility, and no discussion of regulatory, bias, privacy, or deployment limitations for a high-stakes medical application.

The 'omni-modal' framing is overstated: the method only handles image, text, and video; omics and other clinical modalities mentioned in the abstract are not used, and future work is required to include them.
Qualitative examples in Figure 3 are selective and not accompanied by quantitative error analysis, so they do not robustly establish superiority over baselines.
The paper uses 'GPT-5' for benchmark generation and answer rephrasing, which is not reproducible and raises concerns about evaluation stability and dependence on a proprietary model.
No code or model checkpoints are mentioned, limiting reproducibility, and the manuscript defers many details to supplementary material that is not visible in the main paper.
